research_text:
## Factual research brief

### 1. What `SSLContext` governs, and what the reported finding refers to

`javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` represents a secure-socket protocol implementation and acts as a factory for `SSLSocketFactory`, `SSLServerSocketFactory`, and `SSLEngine` instances. It carries configuration and shared state for objects created from it, including key/trust-manager configuration and session state.  
Official sources:  
`https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html`  
`https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html` ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

The detector text refers specifically to the first argument of:

`SSLContext.init(KeyManager[] km, TrustManager[] tm, SecureRandom random)`

That `km` argument supplies sources of local authentication keys. The API documentation permits it to be `null`; if it is null, installed security providers are searched for a highest-priority appropriate factory implementation. The documentation also says only the first manager of a particular key-manager implementation type in the array is used. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

For the cited CrySL rule, the related condition is not an API exception or a TLS-handshake outcome. It is the rule’s required analysis predicate:

`generatedKeyManagers[km];`

The rule itself does **not** mention `KeyManagerFactory`, nor does it define what evidence establishes `generatedKeyManagers[km]`. Therefore, from this rule source alone, the precise detector wording—“was not observed coming from a KeyManagerFactory”—cannot be equated with an official Java API requirement or with a runtime certificate-validation result. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

---

### 2. Officially documented usage and remediation information

#### Documented usage

The Java API documents these supported choices for `SSLContext.init`:

* Supply `KeyManager[]`, `TrustManager[]`, and a `SecureRandom`.
* Supply `null` for either manager array, in which case the installed providers are searched for the appropriate factory implementation.
* Supply `null` for `SecureRandom`, in which case the default implementation is used. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

`KeyManagerFactory` is the documented factory for key managers based on key material, typically a `KeyStore` or a provider-specific source. After initialization, `getKeyManagers()` returns one manager for each type of key material. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/KeyManagerFactory.html))

The JSSE guide explicitly documents **two** origins for `KeyManager` objects: a `KeyManagerFactory` **or a concrete implementation of the interface**. Thus, a manager array not created by a `KeyManagerFactory` is not, by itself, outside the documented Java API contract. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

Similarly, `TrustManagerFactory` is documented as producing trust managers from certificate authorities and related trust material; its initialized `getTrustManagers()` method returns the relevant manager array. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html))

The official JSSE guide’s illustrative TLS setup initializes a key-manager factory and trust-manager factory from key/trust material, then passes their returned arrays to `SSLContext.init`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

#### What the official sources do—and do not—recommend as remediation

The examined official Java sources **do not state that every `KeyManager[]` passed to `SSLContext.init` must originate from a `KeyManagerFactory`**, and they do not prescribe a remediation merely because static analysis cannot establish that provenance.

They do document the factory-based approach as the standard provider-oriented route when key material is sourced from a `KeyStore` or provider-specific key-material source:

1. initialize `KeyManagerFactory` with its applicable source of key material;
2. obtain the array through `getKeyManagers()`;
3. use that array when initializing the context. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/KeyManagerFactory.html))

However, the same JSSE guide explicitly permits a concrete `KeyManager` implementation. Consequently, replacing a custom manager solely to satisfy a provenance predicate is **not an API-mandated migration** according to the official sources reviewed. Any custom manager’s authentication behavior remains an application/provider design question not resolved by `SSLContext`’s factory APIs. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

The API also documents `SSLContext.getDefault()` as returning an immediately usable default context. The CrySL rule forbids that event, but that prohibition is a rule-specific constraint, not an indication that the Java API declares `getDefault()` invalid. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

---

### 3. Compatibility, formats, version support, and documented migration path

#### Persisted formats

The examined `SSLContext` API documentation does **not** define a persisted `SSLContext` format, serialization format, or a persisted-manager-array format. It describes `SSLContext` as runtime configuration/state used to create secure sockets and engines; it does not specify data migration when the provenance of `KeyManager[]` changes. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

A `KeyManagerFactory` may obtain material from a `KeyStore` or provider-specific source, but the factory and `SSLContext` documentation reviewed do not prescribe a keystore-format conversion or any persisted-data migration as part of changing from a custom `KeyManager` to factory-produced managers. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/KeyManagerFactory.html))

#### TLS wire compatibility

The `SSLContext` protocol argument identifies the protocol implementation requested from a provider. It is not itself documentation of the protocol ultimately enabled or negotiated on a particular connection. JSSE documents that enabled protocols are controlled at the `SSLSocket`, `SSLServerSocket`, or `SSLEngine` level through enabled-protocol configuration; provider defaults and disabled-algorithm policy also matter. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

Accordingly, an `SSLContext.getInstance("TLS")` request must not be interpreted, from this API alone, as evidence of negotiating any particular legacy or modern TLS version. Likewise, the CrySL rule’s exact string constraint on `"TLSv1.2"` or `"TLSv1.3"` is a rule condition on the requested argument, not a documented observation of a completed connection’s negotiated protocol. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

The JSSE guide does document material TLS 1.3 interoperability differences: TLS 1.3 has different close behavior, certificate-signature constraints, cipher-suite names/support, and session-resumption/key-update behavior compared with TLS 1.2 and earlier. These considerations concern a change in enabled/negotiated TLS version, not merely changing how the `KeyManager[]` is obtained. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

#### Platform-version support

`SSLContext` has existed since Java 1.4. The current Java SE 25 API states that every Java platform implementation is required to support `TLSv1.2` and `TLSv1.3`; a provider can support additional protocol names. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

For Oracle JDK specifically, TLS 1.3 was introduced in JDK 11 and enabled by default there. Therefore, compatibility with deployments before JDK 11 or with alternative providers cannot be inferred merely from the current Java SE 25 specification; support must be checked against the relevant runtime/provider documentation.  
Official source: `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/migrate/security-updates.html` ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/migrate/security-updates.html?utm_source=openai))

#### Documented migration path

The examined official sources provide no dedicated migration procedure for changing a `KeyManager[]` from a direct implementation to one returned by `KeyManagerFactory`. They document API construction options, including both factory-produced and concrete managers, but not a required transition or compatibility procedure between them. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

---

### 4. Exact matching rule in the supplied CrySL source

Source examined:  
`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl`

The following is the relevant matching and condition text, quoted verbatim:

```text
SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext

FORBIDDEN
	getDefault() => Get;

EVENTS
	g1: getInstance(protocol);
	g2: getInstance(protocol, _);
	Get := g1 | g2;

	i1: init(km, tm, random);
	Init := i1;

	se1: eng = createSSLEngine();
	se2: eng = createSSLEngine(_,_);
	Engine := se1 | se2;

ORDER
	Get, Init, Engine?
CONSTRAINTS
	protocol in {"TLSv1.2", "TLSv1.3"};

REQUIRES
	generatedKeyManagers[km];
	generatedTrustManagers[tm];
	randomized[random];
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

#### What it matches

* **Receiver/API type named by the rule:** `javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`, through the verbatim declaration `SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`.
* **Forbidden method event:** `getDefault()` with no parameters, mapped as `=> Get`.
* **`Get` events:**
  * `getInstance(protocol)` — one parameter, bound to `protocol`;
  * `getInstance(protocol, _)` — two parameters; the first is bound to `protocol`, while the second is unconstrained by `_`.
* **`Init` event:** `init(km, tm, random)` — three parameters, bound to the declared objects `km`, `tm`, and `random`.
* **`Engine` events:**
  * `eng = createSSLEngine()` — zero arguments;
  * `eng = createSSLEngine(_,_)` — two arguments, both unconstrained by `_`.

Thus, the rule **does constrain the parameter lists** of the events it declares: their arity is represented by the event signatures, and selected positions are bound to named objects or marked `_`. The rule’s explicit `CONSTRAINTS` condition is:

```text
protocol in {"TLSv1.2", "TLSv1.3"};
```

It also requires the three predicates:

```text
generatedKeyManagers[km];
generatedTrustManagers[tm];
randomized[random];
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

#### Can it match a method that merely shares an API method name?

**No, not according to the text of this rule.** The source scopes the specification to the fully qualified type:

```text
SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext
```

The rule source does not state that a same-named method on an unrelated receiver type is in scope. It supplies no alternate receiver type and no name-only matching declaration. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

## Source limitations and unresolved questions

* The CrySL URL uses `refs/heads/master`, which is mutable. The supplied SHA-256 value was not independently verified against an immutable commit or compiled rule artifact.
* `SSLContext.crysl` does not define the semantics or producer of `generatedKeyManagers[km]`; it only requires that predicate. Establishing whether a particular analysis engine recognizes a given origin requires the detector version, compiled ruleset, and diagnostic trace.
* The official Java sources permit both factory-produced and direct concrete `KeyManager` implementations. They do not state that a factory is universally required, nor do they provide a mandated migration path for provenance-only findings.
* The reviewed API documentation does not establish actual enabled protocols, negotiated TLS version, certificate validation behavior, hostname-verification behavior, or provider-specific compatibility for any particular application.
